speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam asked me three questions relating to the export of automobile parts to China, and I should like to answer them seriatim.
First, he asked if I had received any complaints from Canadian exporters with regard to the refusal of automobile companies in Canada which are subsidiaries of United States automobile manufacturers to supply automotive parts for export to China. As I said yesterday, I was unaware of any complaints but I found that last summer I had received a complaint from one Canadian exporter, whose name I believe was Mr. Grinkus of Gain Import Company Limited, who was unable to obtain a supply of certain types of automotive parts for export to mainland China, stating that the difficulties experienced were attributable to a refusal of subsidiaries in Canada of United States automobile manufacturers to supply parts for export to China.
The second question asked whether this refusal is based upon the declared policy of the United States government. In reply to that I would only say that no information is available on this matter other than that provided at the time by that exporter. Accordingly I have some difficulty in answering the question whether there has been such a refusal on the part of the automobile manufacturers in question and, if so, what their reason may have been.
His third question asked if so, does the minister consider this action to be a violation of Canada's right to exercise control over its own economy? If the parts concerned had been of United States origin, of course no Canadian export permit would have been given for their re-export to mainland China. This is the policy of the Canadian government, and I do not think in any sense it is a violation of Canada's right to control its own economy. This is the exercise of its own right. If the parts were of Canadian origin it is possible, although I have no information other than that provided by the exporter himself, that they might have been available from sources in the market other than the manufacturers which are subsidiaries of United States companies. However, [Mr. Caouette.l
one of the difficulties in answering this question is that we have no information on this other than the word of the exporter himself.
May I add this, Mr. Speaker. As the hon. member may be aware, arrangements were agreed to some years ago between the United States and Canadian governments for consideration to be given by the United States government to an application for a foreign assets control licence by a United States parent company arising out of a transaction which might have been consummated in Canada. In recent years there has been no request from a Canadian automobile manufacturer for our intercession in support of a parent company's application for an F.A.C. licence, and accordingly it may be that the companies have other reasons if they have refused to supply the exporter in question.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to direct a question to the Prime Minister. I do so as a socialist but also one not ashamed upon occasion and under certain circumstances to be a monarchist. I desire to ask the Prime Minister if his attention has been drawn to the following statement which appeared in the March 23 issue of the Montreal newspaper Le Devoir:
The army of liberation of Quebec has "ordered" yesterday the Queen not to present herself on Quebec territory.. ."unless she is aspiring at being the first British sovereign to die on the Quebec earth".
Although similar questions have been asked before, I ask this question because in spite of all the security measures taken in the United States, a fanatic killed the president. In Canada we do not want a fanatic of any kind killing the Queen of Canada and the commonwealth. In view of these continued threats I ask the Prime Minister what special attention is being given to the matter of whether or not the Queen should come to Canada, particularly to Quebec, and what protection will be afforded her in view of all these threats.

subtopic: REPORTED DANGER TO QUEEN IN QUEBEC

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, March 23, consideration of the motion of Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance), that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Nowlan.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes still at my disposal before I conclude my remarks, I should like to make some observations concerning federal-provincial relations.
The vague allegations by the minister on that matter leave us puzzled. As a matter of fact, it is enough to wonder whether the government is not preparing a new centralizing offensive which will certainly come to light at the opening of the conference on March 31 next.
The doings of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) in rushing through the budget, only a few weeks before that conference, are bound to give rise to most serious doubts. We wonder why such haste to introduce a budget which is much more noteworthy by its omissions than by its contents.
It seems that even the date chosen for the introduction of the budget speech is an affront to the provinces. Yet, at last November's conference, the attitude of the provinces was clearly set out and could be resumed as follows:
1.	Systematic objection to any federal action which in fact curtails the field of provincial jurisdiction.
2.	Absolute opposition to any unilateral federal action which is bound to upset provincial priorities, particularly in the case of area development.
3.	Since economic problems seldom come under exclusive federal jurisdiction, the provinces should be consulted every time decisions are taken which might affect their economy.


4.	Participation in one way or another, through permanent federal-provincial agencies set up for that purpose, in the determination of any federal policy likely to affect the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, such is the very clear position which was proposed not only by the government of the province of Quebec, but by the governments of several other provinces. As a matter of fact, if we refer to the press release which was issued after that conference, it seems indeed that the federal government had agreed on those view points, because it states that a thorough consultation must take place about the measures it is deemed advisable to pass and, for that purpose, it suggests the setting up of a system which will make possible such close and permanent consultation and will make sure that all governments will have all the required authority to assume their respective responsibilities.
So that the words co-operative federalism will not be mere window dressing to cover a fool's agreement, I direct the following questions to the Minister of Finance:
Why have not the necessary provisions been passed yet to implement those objectives?
Why were not steps taken to make it easier for the provinces who so desire to withdraw from joint programs, and why are new joint programs being developed?
In view of the provisions of the budget itself, will it be possible to make new fiscal arrangements that will meet the demands of the provinces?
Why did not the Minister of Finance consult his provincial colleagues before preparing his budget?
And, finally, what positive provisions have been taken, or are going to be taken by the government to carry out the various suggestions and recommendations not only from this side of the house, but from all its corners, tending to establish a sound federalism, and more particularly the following suggestions:
The immediate establishment of an adequate permanent federal-provincial secretariat, which might group in its set-up all the various agencies for federal-provincial consultation.
The setting up of a constitutional Senate committee, as was suggested the other day by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer).
The repatriation of our constitution and its adjustment to modern needs, which would, again, answer the exigencies of a sound federalism.

The setting up of a constitutional court, which as a last resort would decide any possible disputes between the provinces and the federal government, as well as all constitutional differences.
And, lastly, which is perhaps a new suggestion, the establishment by the House of Commons of a standing committee responsible for matters which, perhaps, more particularly affect the province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, until we get satisfactory answers from the Minister of Finance, I respectfully submit that it is useless to speak of co-operation, of co-operative federalism, and that our confederation system will never run smoothly.
In closing, I must say that budget does not look like a real budget to me, but just a provisional one, drawn up hastily and which brings no real solution to current problems. Mr. Speaker, finally, I suggest that the minister, now that he has had a little time to think about those questions and the opportunity to hear the views of the members of this house, get down to work earnestly and come up with a real budget-let him call it supplementary or whatever he likes-in order to fill once and for all the painful gaps left by his first abortive attempt.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like first of all to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) for the Easter tints he has given his budget. The sentence which impressed me the most in the budget, the one he read most enthusiastically and most emphatically is the following:
All hon. members can take satisfaction from the improvement that has been occurring in economic conditions in Canada and from the optimism with which we can view the immediate future.
Mr. Speaker, we could piously add Alleluia, and all the Easter spirit would be there.
On the other hand, there are other parts of his speech that are a little more in accordance with Passiontide. In certain parts of his speech, the Minister of Finance reminded us of a son who, having pitifully failed an exam, is telling his father about his results. The father is quite sad, but suddenly in a cheerful tone he says to his son: "I congratulate you because at least I am sure that you did not cheat."
Evidently the Minister of Finance did not cheat when he prepared this budget. He admitted it himself, he did not ask the advice of any expert, he did not annoy anyone, and what he presented was pure traditionalism.
However, I wish to say to the Minister of Finance that I was in a somewhat nostalgic mood when I heard him read his budget this year. Last year he came like an eager zealot who had undertaken the conquest of the
The Budget-Mr. Girouard powerful capitalists. I must admit that he had succeeded in stirring up their wrath and that he must have been sorry.
The 1963 budget was perhaps a political disaster for the Liberal party, but for the Minister of Finance himself, it was a sign of greatness. I had a higher opinion of the Minister of Finance in difficulty than I do now when I see him entirely satisfied with the insignificant budget he has just introduced.
Mr. Speaker, the 1963 budget had made few people happy, but it had at least called for sympathy and friendliness. It was good to see a minister reveal himself as an idealist, since he was not young maybe, but new to public office. I know that at the time, he won the admiration of many young members of his party. The minister now introduces a budget which shows that he no longer wants to break new ground. But there is still in him a strain of candour that borders on naivete. "Let us rejoice", he says, but he goes on: "Unemployment is still too high, and in the Atlantic provinces and eastern Quebec it is much too high". He admits it and I recognize that he is frank, but he goes on to say, and this is terrific:
At the beginning of this year the seasonally adjusted figure for unemployment in Canada was just below 5 per cent. However, according to our best current estimates, the figure for British Columbia, again on a seasonally adjusted basis, was just above 4 per cent. For the prairies it was around 2 per cent. In Ontario it had fallen to about 3 per cent, but in Quebec, where the increase in the labour force had been quite exceptional, it was probably about 6 per cent. For the Atlantic region, the figure while falling, was probably still as high as 8 per cent.
I should like to call the attention of the house to the various degrees of assurance used by the Minister of Finance when introducing his statistics. In British Columbia the Minister of Finance is certain, he gives the assurance thataccording to our best current estimates, again on a seasonally adjusted basisunemployment was just above 4 per cent. For the prairies, he is also sure that unemployment is around 2 per cent. In Ontario, he also says flatly that unemployment has fallen to about 3 per cent. But in Quebec the minister is no longer quite sure- neither in the maritime provinces. First he says thatthe increase in the labour force has been quite exceptional.
He does not say how this is done, but it is very unusual. However, it seems that the unemployment rate is 6 to 8 per cent. The minister certainly knows that the percentage has decreased in the maritime provinces, and that it is now 8 per cent. That is about it.
Nevertheless, I would like to ask the minister to explain why these statistics are

The Budget-Mr. Girouard unreliable. Is it not the same experts who compile statistics throughout the country? I would like especially to point out to him and to the government that even though experts are not the same, provinces are, areas are, as are also the workers who have been unemployed for six years.
That is not all, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of Finance went on:
The wide diversity of these figures and the prospect for the current year suggest that broad, general attacks on unemployment will be less useful now-
That beats everything, Mr. Speaker. Reference is made to broad general attacks on unemployment, while I am given to understand that in Quebec province there is 6 per cent unemployment, and 8 per cent in the maritimes.
The minister continued:
Accordingly, our plans and policies are increasingly designed to meet the special needs of areas of the country or groups of the population confronted with special difficulties and problems.
There you are. The Minister of Finance has settled the problem. Unemployment is decreasing in western Canada and they say it is because of the far reaching operation by the government. But if unemployment is decreasing in western Canada, it is because of a far reaching operation, but not an operation by the government. It is because of a far reaching operation by Russia, China and other European countries who simply launched the operation "we want bread".
One might think that the government deserves to be commended for having lent a friendly ear to that request? Not at all, Mr. Speaker, because the sale of wheat to communist countries and to European countries was an initiative of the Conservative party.
Indeed, when such action was taken last year, it was among the cries and objections of those who want to take all the credit for it today.
Therefore, I wonder what has become of the "large scale operation of the Liberal party." The Liberal party was to launch a far reaching operation, and what was done actually about it? During the last election it faced a Conservative party which offered wheat sales, vast trade outlets, a winter works scheme, and public works to help the municipalities, new and easier facilities from the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and ARDA. In spite of all these measures, things did not work out the way the Canadian public wanted, people wished to change their government.
Now, let us see what the Liberal party has given Canada since it took over. We had the winter works program, and the first action


the government took in this field was to cut the winter works period. Yet, how many promises had been made with regard to this matter. Each hon. member rose, at one time or another, to ask whether there was no possibility of extending the winter works period. I also rose in the house to ask the minister whether there was any possibility of extending the winter works period in some districts, but I was told that nothing could be done. It is certainly not in the field of winter works that I can note far reaching policies.
Now, what has been the government's policy concerning grants to underdeveloped areas? Much publicity has been made on this subject of underdeveloped areas. Grants were increased by 10 per cent to help them. This did not work either. Why? Because when the municipalities do not even have enough money to buy materials, what use have they for the money offered by Ottawa to pay wages?
There was also this situation-in my own constituency more particularly-on which I want again to call the attention of the house. Four parishes had considerable public works to be done, and they wanted at least to take advantage of this assistance granted by the federal government to underdeveloped areas. Again I wrote to the minister, saying: there are only four parishes in my constituency which do not benefit from the assistance the government grants to underdeveloped areas; would it not be possible to allow these four parishes to benefit from that governmental assistance? Do you know what reply I got? It makes me laugh. I was told: "These four parishes are indeed in your constituency, but they do not come under the same unemployment insurance office. To grant them the same advantages would occasion administrative problems." This is exactly what the Minister of Finance was saying last year.
So, even when I examine the government's assistance program to underdeveloped areas,
I	see nothing of that famous far reaching operation. But I am going to give the government more chances. I shall take a close look at some other of its objectives.
Is it in the building industry that we had a far reaching operation by the government? Well, the government surely did something in the building field. It levied a tax on materials and today they boast that construction was very high this winter. But I hope they will not have the effrontery to pretend that if construction improved, it was because of the new tax on building materials.
If construction was active this winter, it is because people decided to take advantage of the 4 per cent tax before it is raised to 8 or
II	per cent. Mr. Speaker, when this tax on

building materials reaches its maximum level, the government will no longer believe it was a far reaching operation.
Where was it felt that far reaching operation was supposed to provide full employment? Again, the Liberal party was duty bound to promote full employment because specific pledges had been made in this respect, and that is why the Conservative party was defeated at the last federal election. The Liberal party had made all kinds of pledges in this connection but today what have we got: complete failure. Well, I know that the Liberal party had great undertakings in some fields. But I want to tell them that in this day and age, Canadians are very much interested in our foreign affairs, but they are also very much interested in the problems related to defence, especially the citizens in my riding, where a base has been built in La Macaza which is the finest monument to our subjection to the United States. Canadians are also interested in bilingualism and biculturalism, especially in the province of Quebec where, for once, fire defeated ashes. But if Canadians are that interested in all those accomplishments of the Liberal party, it is as long as they can sit at night, with a full stomach, before their television sets to read their newspapers.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance tells us there are 6 per cent of unemployed in the province of Quebec. This figure can represent as much as 100,000 heads of families which have inadequate housing, clothing and food. However, as I have said, the minister in this atmosphere of well-being continues to talk about "the optimism with which we can view the immediate future".
Now, if one considers the unemployment problem, one realizes that the large scale operations in this field by the government since the Liberal party came into office, are highly questionable.
Let us consider the farming situation. I would not like the Minister of Finance to forget that farmers are also in the Easter season. I would not like to do like the former member for Bellechasse who, every time he rose, said he spoke on the part of the 92,000 farmers in eastern Canada whose income is below $1200 a year. I would not like to repeat that to no avail, but the situation is serious. I certainly should like to know what the government has achieved in the way of large-scale operations to assist eastern farmers.
In my constituency, as well as in the province as a whole, only one farm out of three can keep on operating at the present time and, if it can manage to do so, it is because the head of the family goes off by himself to find a job somewhere else. And if at any time he should be unlucky enough to lose that job, 20220-90
The Budget-Mr. Girouard well, on top of that, he is not even entitled to unemployment insurance benefits, because then he is told: "You are a farmer". Where then is that wonderful large scale operation the Liberal party was supposed to carry out to promote eastern agriculture?
I could quote statistics and give examples, but that would not change the situation a bit, for I am convinced that each and every one of us is familiar with the problems of our eastern farmers. They are so well acquainted with them that they should have found a solution during the last election campaign.
It had been said that the member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Tremblay) would be the next minister of agriculture for eastern Canada. It seemed serious enough, because the hon. member had announced it himself. But later, when a member of the opposition-
I think it was the member for Joliette-L'As-somption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon)-pressed the government to say when the minister of agriculture would be appointed, the member for Lotbiniere rose to his feet and cockily said: "One minister of agriculture will not be sufficient, we want two departments". And now, the member for Matapedia-Matane has become a specialist in railroads which remain unbuilt. But we have no department nor minister of agriculture for eastern Canada.
I see no mention of large scale projects put forward by the government for the benefit of eastern farmers. Who will take the matter in hand then, I ask you?
The other day, the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent) gave me dreadful examples showing why the Department of Agriculture in Ottawa is completely unaware of the problems of Quebec farmers. Since the government likes so much to set up commissions and to advertise widely its accomplishments, I think it would be time to launch an investigation on farm problems in eastern Canada.
A great number of my constituents, including many farmers, ask me what I might possibly do for them in Ottawa. I was able to do little if anything for them. The case of one of my electors has been of particular interest to me. His name is Mr. St. Pierre, he lives in my riding and he came to see me one day to talk about a farm loan application he had made. The agronomists had looked over his land and they had advised him to apply for a loan, telling him that he had a very good chance to get it as he met all the requirements. But Mr. St. Pierre did not get his farm loan.
This may be of interest to the house, although I do not want to establish any relation between the two things but the inspector who looked over Mr. St. Pierre's land
1412	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Girouard was the brother-in-law of the Liberal candidate I defeated. And Mr. St. Pierre was one of my supporters. I do not want necessarily to establish any relations between these two facts. However, I submit that if the government wanted to set up a royal commission on that matter it would get very interesting information.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, I ask the government who will act for the eastern farmers in future, and in what way?
But, Mr. Speaker, it might be that unemployment and agriculture are not such important problems for the government. We note how successful it has been in other fields. And the minister continues:
The deficit in our current account balance of payments with other countries is still too large but it is smaller than it has been since 1954.
Mr. Speaker, should we then congratulate the Liberal party which laughed at the Conservative party, saying that the dollar was worth only 92.5 cents. Today, the government seems to say: It is thanks to us if the trade balance righted itself.
Come now. It is a well known fact that the improvement in the trade balance is due to the action taken by the former minister of trade and commerce, Mr. George Hees.
On what does the Liberal party deserve to be commended? Perhaps in connection with federal-provincial relations, according to the statement made by the minister when he said:
But now the public expects so much from both levels of government that they often appear to be in competition with one another.
I often wonder whether it is the public who expects everything from both levels of government or if it is not rather the federal politicians who find it very profitable to take advantage of the public during an election campaign.
I appreciate that the provinces have needs in the fields of education, assistance to the municipalities and social legislation, but when the people have requests to make along those lines, they address themselves to the proper authorities.
However, during election campaigns, politicians profess their willingness to help the people. It looks good to promise scholarships and municipal loans because it brings votes. Yet, it is the public which must bear the burden of the uneven distribution of revenues between the two levels of government.
The burden is so unevenly distributed today that we are now in the midst of a constitutional chaos.
To get out of it, two alternatives seem possible: either we break resolutely through the constitutional walls, or go under them. 

The latter alternative is what the Secretary of State calls co-operative federalism. But if the government is able to pay out $10 to every student across the country, if it is able to set up a municipal loans fund, if the government goes into provincial fields, where is he going to get all the money? From the provinces, it is as simple as that.
I am wondering if it would not be much simpler for the Minister of Finance to abide by the constitution and allow the provinces themselves to collect these $10 and to distribute them.
If the federal parties have not enough promises left, may I suggest a few to them. In the field of external affairs, the federal politicians could travel about and promise peace, they might even promise the appointment of an ambassador to the Vatican. As far as defence is concerned, they could travel about and promise disarmament, and to do so, I give them my permission to demolish the Bomarcs stored in my riding; this would create jobs for the unemployed. In the postal field, they could promise a well-organized rural service and in the municipalities, a more efficient home delivery service.
There you have the best promises a federal party could make and that would be much better than tampering with the constitution.
I would not care to swim against the current all the time, but there is one idea I should like to put forth concerning what is constitutionally legal in all those federal-provincial agreements. We have reached the point where provincial premiers meet and decide to amend the constitution. Now, that is something which belongs to the people and which only the people can amend.
All members of the house should ponder over the fact that it is not up to a province to amend the constitution, but to a whole people, and that the normal way to proceed in such a case is to hold a referendum.
Since the constitution must be amended, let us do it as soon as possible. Let us repatriate it and amend it. Many suggestions will be made and some minorities will fear that, in so doing, the majority will gain the upper hand. There are several possible solutions in that respect, but even if the latter is adopted, it must be remembered that to carry out such a project, the provinces must get together and give their unanimous consent, otherwise each province could appeal to the supreme court. However, it would be possible to protect the rights of individuals.
Mr. Speaker, I shall summarize my remarks by calling four or five points to the attention of the government.
Things have not started rolling as far as unemployment is concerned; must we have

confidence in the government? The condition of agriculture is still unsatisfactory but, there again, must we trust the government? The national defence situation is not as it should be; must we have confidence in the government in that respect and also as concerns biculturalism?
That is the only thing we do, trust the government. We have been placing our trust in the government for a year now and we are expected to go on doing so.
I can assure you of one thing. The more we trust the government and the longer it takes to act, all the harsher will Canadians be towards the Liberals when they go to the polls. It will not be able to say that it has gone through a difficult period. But if the Liberal party cannot accomplish miracles, let it stop pretending that it can work miracles.
I hope that during the few years it has left it will mend its ways and do more than it has done since we have been sitting here.

Mr. Speaker, before speaking about the amendment that is before the house I should like to say something about the economic measures that were taken by the government last spring and summer and the economic policies that have been followed since that time; about the economic objectives enunciated in the budget speech, and about the present economic outlook in Canada. First of all let me review the economic policies and the economic measures that have been introduced by the government, and their effects so far.
The first one to which I should like to refer -and they are not in any particular order- is the $500 winter house building bonus program. The purpose of this measure was to even out to some extent the seasonal peaks and valleys in employment in the house building industry; to provide more jobs, in other words, during the winter months. Mr. Speaker, hon. members of the house may remember that this program was ridiculed last spring as a gimmick, but the measure has proved to be eminently successful. As an example, housing starts in the months of December, 1962 and January, 1963 were 12,009; for December, 1963 and January, 1964 housing starts were 24,191, or more than double the number of the year before.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

The second point in this general connection which helps people to improve their skills and which is provided for in the budget is the provision that tuition fees of part-time students may be deducted from taxable income; and the third is the proposal that loans on an interest-free basis should be made to university students. I think that we on this side of the house feel very pleased and satisfied that we were in a position to bring in these three measures which will do something for the younger people of this country.
The fifth measure I wish to mention is the incentives provided last year to stimulate activity in areas of slower growth. This is another policy that was ridiculed by the opposition when it was first announced, perhaps because it was new and untried in Canada. About 150 inquiries respecting possible projects for designated areas have so far been handled by the area development agency. Of these, 34 companies have formally indicated that they will go ahead with projects to be located in 14 of the 35 designated areas. They involve a capital investment of over $73.5 million and are expected to provide some 5,000 new jobs. The indications are that the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) will 

shortly be asked to certify new projects representing another $100 million or so . in capital investment.
The extension of the tax concession in designated areas to April 1, 1967 has been greeted with enthusiasm. If I may, I should like to quote a letter which I received from Mr. W. N. Hall, president of Dominion Tar and Chemical Company Limited whose head office is in Montreal. He says:
I should like to express my thanks and congratulations to you on the inclusion in the budget of an extension of the tax concessions in designated areas to April 1, 1967.
My thanks are on account of the fact that I believe the concessions will be most helpful in allowing this company to do some things which otherwise would not be possible, and my congratulations are because I am sure this extension will bring needed industry to a number of areas which would not get industry on a normal taxation basis.
The sixth measure to which I wish to refer is the creation of the municipal development and loan board. There are 107 loans to date under this program amounting to $42.5 million, the largest of which so far is a loan of $29 million to metropolitan Toronto. I expect most applications under this act will be made this year, 1964, although the effects of increased employment resulting from them will continue until March 1966. As hon. members will recall, when the bill leading to the Municipal Development and Loan Act was being debated it was made clear that it was an intermediate program, or that its effects would be for the intermediate period. Most municipalities had already established their capital budgets for the calendar year 1963 and it was thought unlikely that many of them would be able to take advantage of these additional credit facilities during the 1963 year. We are now finding that municipalities are beginning to take advantage of the credit made available under the act for 1964.
The seventh measure to which I would like to refer is the Atlantic development board. Projects approved to date include, first, a power development at Mactaquac, New Brunswick, amounting to some $20 million. Another $20 million is being spent on the power development at bay d'Espoir in Newfoundland-I believe that is the correct way to pronounce the word in Newfoundland, if not in some other parts of Canada. Third, assistance is being provided for basic facilities for the fishing industry at Georgetown, Prince Edward Island; and the fourth project so far is assistance for basic facilities, again for the fisheries, at Canso, Nova Scotia. I personally am delighted that this measure to improve the basic economic structure of the Atlantic area is taking hold. The Atlantic development fund is the outcome of a recommendation made in the fall of 1956 by a royal

commission of which I had the honour to be chairman. It has taken a long time, some people might think too long, to act on the recommendations of that commission, but we are now beginning to get somewhere. If it results in an improvement in economic conditions in the Atlantic area I am sure all members of the house and all people in the country will be more than pleased.
The eighth point I would like to make is in connection with the monetary policy that has been pursued and the spread between interest rates in Canada and the United States. During 1963 the operations of the Bank of Canada were directed towards encouraging credit conditions in a way which would help to strengthen and sustain the expansion of the Canadian economy.
Interest rates in the United States rose moderately during the course of 1963, and I think that the real phenomenon is that the spread between United States and Canadian rates narrowed appreciably. There seems to be general agreement with the monetary policy that has been followed, and it is one of the reasons why the Canadian economy has been expanding.
These various policies and measures are paying off. They are working well and they will continue to work well. All of them have contributed directly to the improvement in our economic picture.
Before leaving this subject I should like to say a word, more or less in parenthesis, about the older workers program. This program was not expected to be the final answer to the employment problem of older workers, and for that reason it was introduced on an experimental basis. The program was designed to assist employers during the period an eligible older worker was given the training and work experience necessary for his continued employment.
In some cases difficulty was experienced in finding workers to fill approved job vacancies, because the types of work offered were not attractive to many of the workers who were suitable for referral to the particular employers concerned. In other cases there was some shortage of eligible older workers who could meet the specifications of the job openings. But up to the end of February 1964 there were 1,986 applications from employers submitted to the national employment service offices. Of this number 1,333 had been approved, and by the end of February 936 eligible older workers had been placed in jobs.
There was a considerable increase in both applications and placements under the program during the month of February. Inquiries also increased in volume, indicating that further increases might be expected in March, the last month of the hiring period.
The Budget

Mr. Gordon The other day the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) referred to the number of older workers placed in jobs up to the end of January, and he compared this figure with the cost of an advertising program to inform people of the older workers scheme that had just been started about that time.
He rather ridiculed the cost of the advertising in relation to the number of people who had been placed in jobs prior to the insertion of the advertisements, in other words, prior to the time most people knew the older workers program was in existence. In reply I would just like to say that the advertising program seems to have been effective. To the extent that this program has been and is being successful, it means the re-establishment as useful members of society of men who had been forgotten, men who had been made to feel they were not needed in our modern age. To the extent we are able to do something about this in one way or another it seems to me we are moving in the right direction. I have said something about the various economic policies and measures which have had considerable to do with the improvement in conditions in Canada in the last eight or ten months. I should now like to say a few words about the economic objectives of the government as set out in the budget speech. The first of these is the maintenance of high levels of employment.
Employment in February, 1964, was 272,000 higher than it was a year ago, the biggest increase in many, many years. Unemployment in February, 1964, was 78,000 lower than it was in the same month in the previous year.
Unemployment, as a percentage of the working force, reached its peak in 1961, and has been falling since that time.
The averages by the calendar years over the last decade have been as follows, and I think the trend is of interest: In 1954 the average was 4.6 per cent; in 1955 it was 4.4 per cent; in 1956 it was 3.4 per cent; in 1957 it was 4.6 per cent; in 1958 it was 7.1 per cent; in 1959 it was 6.0 per cent; in 1960 it was 7.0 per cent; in 1961 it was 7.2 per cent; in 1962 it was 5.9 per cent, and in 1963 it was 5.5 per cent.
The more recent improvement is greater than the yearly averages indicate. The following monthly figures show this on a seasonally adjusted basis. In July, 1963, unemployment was 5.9 per cent of the working force on a seasonally adjusted basis. In August it was 5.4 per cent. In September and October it was 5.3 per cent. In November it was 5.1 per cent, and in December, 1963, and to January, 1964, it was 4.9 per cent. In February of this year it was 4.7 per cent.

I am perfectly prepared to agree with the hon. member who spoke a few minutes ago that these rates are still far too high. I am not satisfied with the situation where unemployment in Canada is at a seasonally adjusted rate of 4.7 per cent. I am sure all other hon. members of the house are not satisfied either, but at least the curve is moving downwards and we can take some satisfaction from that. We must make sure in our policies and programs that we keep the curve moving downward in the months and years ahead.

speechtext:
No juggling; just planning. The third objective is an expansion of international trade and a reduction in the deficit on current account. The deficit on our current account with other countries was $521 million in 1963, again too high but the lowest since 1954. This country must do everything possible to push our exports so that the deficit in our current account transactions will be brought down to a reasonable balance.
In this connection and because it is vitally necessary to push our exports, perhaps I may be permitted to refer to a policy change that was announced last summer to permit the export of hydroelectric power, provided there are proper safeguards for domestic consumers in the future. As a result of this new policy approach it was possible to move on the Columbia river development which unquestionably will be of tremendous value and benefit not only to the people of British Columbia but to the people of Canada as a whole. Second, the government is working with the government of Manitoba in examining the power potential of the Nelson river to see if


it can be developed at a cost which will permit very large and substantial exports either to the United States or possibly, depending on the circumstances, to Ontario. If the Ontario hydro commission should become really interested in this development on the Nelson it might take some of its future power requirements from that source and as a result reduce the need for imported coal for thermal plants. This would have the same effect as increased exports in so far as the current account deficit is concerned. Finally, there is the great potential development on the Hamilton river about which I should like to say a word or two in a minute.
The fourth objective of economic policy is to maintain reasonable stability in prices and the value of our currency. There has been a lot of comment, quite exaggerated comment if I may say so, about price stability in recent months. I might perhaps give a few comparisons of the changes in the consumer price indices in Canada and other countries between December, 1962, and December, 1963. In the United States consumer prices increased by
1.7	per cent during that 12 month period and in Canada the increase was exactly the same,
1.7	per cent. In the United Kingdom it was
1.8 per cent, in Sweden it was 2.7 per cent, in Germany 3.7 per cent and the same in Switzerland, in France it was 5.7 per cent, in Japan 5.8 per cent, in Italy it was 7.1 per cent. So on the basis of that kind of comparison we have not been doing badly in Canada.
On the matter of economic objectives there was one other point mentioned in the budget speech which is partly economic and partly political. I refer to the fact that Canada probably has the most open economy of any country in the world. This is to our best advantage. It is in our best interests, and as far as the government is concerned this will be continued. But as I said in the budget speech, there should be "full participation by Canadians in the management and direction of all aspects of our own affairs". I suspect it will not have gone unnoticed that in the budget speech this year I repeated what I said last June about the government's views and objectives concerning foreign owned Canadian subsidiary companies.
A word now, Mr. Speaker, about the economic outlook in Canada. I have already referred to the forecast of growth for 1964, to the fact that unemployment is down and employment up, to the fact that unemployment is now a regional rather than a national problem and is concentrated mainly-I referred to this in the budget speech-in eastern Quebec and the Atlantic provinces.
Apart from the incentives offered to industry to establish new manufacturing and processing plants in areas of slow growth, a

policy which I am very hopeful will bear a great deal of fruit in the next few months, the best thing that could happen from the standpoint of more jobs in eastern Canada would be an early decision to go ahead with the $600 million to $700 million development of the Hamilton falls power project. I would urge all parties concerned with this great enterprise as seriously as I can to work out their differences, if any, and to get ahead with this vitally important project.
The other day the hon. member for Nanai-mo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) suggested that some people had referred to my latest effort as a Tory budget. I must say I winced when I heard that epithet. I have been called a lot of things in my day, not a few of them since I became Minister of Finance, but I cannot remember ever before being called a Tory. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that the powerful stimulants to expansion introduced last year, the effects of which are now beginning to be felt, will continue to be felt, as I have said. Apart from this, and in the kind of economic conditions I have outlined, what other fiscal and economic policies are called for at this time?
It is quite true that there are those who advocate massive tax cuts in order to keep up with the Americans. I cannot accept this as the right prescription in present circumstances, and when I say that I mean the circumstances of mid-March, 1964. If at some later date the forward surge in the economy should show signs of faltering, that would be another matter. But there are no such signs on the horizon now.
Many hon. members have made useful contributions to the debate, although for the most part they seem to have more or less cancelled one another out. I should like to mention two things that were said, the first by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Slogan). He suggested that in order to give vitality to this country we need the vision of 1957. My recollection of the vision, or nightmare, depending on how you like to refer to it, is that it was followed by high average unemployment-in 1958 of 7.1 per cent; in 1959 of 6 percent; in 1960 of 7 per cent and in 1961 of 7.2 per cent. It was followed also by two exchange crises. During that period the whole Canadian economy was in the doldrums.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH CAPITAL PUNISHMENT EXCEPT FOR TREASON
AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH CAPITAL PUNISHMENT EXCEPT FOR TREASON
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-12, to amend the Criminal Code (capital punishment).
He said: The purpose of this bill, second reading of which I am now moving, is to amend the Criminal Code so as to abolish hanging as a penalty for the crime of murder.
Hon. members will notice that I have deliberately not touched upon the subject of treason because for the purpose of discussion this afternoon I wanted to try to limit the debate to the question of hanging as a penalty for the crime of murder. This is a subject upon which debate has raged back and forth for many years. People on either side of the controversy have, I think, held their views with sincerity and conviction and I suppose that no matter what happens to this bill the subject will always be one of which there will be deep differences of opinion among the population.
Those who read Hansard will have observed that the last great debate on this subject took place in 1961 when several days were devoted to a discussion of the matter. I think anyone reading the report is bound to be impressed by the fact that these debates

are probably among the finest to be found in the pages of Hansard. The question we really have to decide this afternoon is, it seems to me, a fairly simple one, namely is hanging an effective deterrent to murder or is there another deterrent which is just as effective and not so drastic? In my few remarks I hope to be able to demonstrate to the house that the penalty of capital punishment cannot be justified upon logical grounds and certainly not on moral grounds, and that there are other deterrents which are just as effective, though less drastic. I should like to divide my argument into two parts. First, I should like to examine briefly the case in favour of retaining capital punishment and, second, to discuss the arguments put forward in favour of its abolition.
The only real argument of substance which is advanced in favour of retaining capital punishment is based upon what is called the theory of deterrence. This is the theory that potential murderers will stop to consider the consequence of their action; that they realize that if apprehended and convicted they will be hanged, and that this will deter them from committing murder. An examination of the evidence in jurisdictions where capital punishment has been abolished in no way supports this theory.
Hon. members will be interested to hear of some of the countries which have abolished capital punishment and the years in which they decided to do so: Holland, 1860; Denmark, 1892; Norway, 1876; Sweden, 1919; and West Germany. There are a host of European and Scandinavian countries which abolished the death penalty before 1900. But in these five particular cases where the penalty has been out of use for about a hundred years it is interesting to compare the murder rate with that of Canada. The latest statistics indicate that the murder rate in Canada is about 1.2 per 100,000. In Holland, the rate is .04; in Norway, it is .05; in Sweden, .08; in Denmark, 1.00 and in West Germany, 1.2. These are, for the most part, jurisdictions where the death penalty has been abolished for about 100 years and in every case except one the murder rate is lower than it is in Canada, while in the remaining case it is no worse.
The figures in the United States are of some assistance. In six states of the United States which have abolished the death penalty, the figures for 1958 indicate that the murder rate was 1.83 per 100,000. In the 42 states which retained it, the murder rate was 7.04. Again, the available statistics indicate that capital punishment has no deterrent value at all. In New Zealand, between 1946 and 1950 when the death penalty was not in existence, the murder rate was 6.7 per 100,000. In 1956,
Criminal Code
when it was reintroduced, the murder rate rose to 8.7. Hon. members can examine any jurisdiction they please. They can take any group of 40 or 50 countries representing both industrial' and rural societies, both developed and underdeveloped nations, or having different levels of education, and still any evidence which is available will indicate that the incidence of murder bears no relationship at all to the existence or non-existence of the penalty of capital punishment.
In any event, the death penalty is very rarely invoked. In the United States, where there are 7,000 murders every year, only some 50 murderers are executed. What is the deterrent value of a penalty which is so rarely invoked? Again, the death penalty is highly discriminatory in its nature. Those most likely to die are the poor, members of minority groups, the unintelligent and the friendless. The warden at Sing Sing who accompanied 149 men to the death chamber reported that in every case they were men who had no money. More than half of all those executed in the United States are Negroes.
The death penalty does not even begin to deal with the vast majority of murders classified as family murders-cases where a wife murders her husband, or the husband murders his wife, or one of them murders the children. The amendment to the Criminal Code introduced in 1961 tried to deal with the subject and it seems to me it is time for us to go all the way and abolish the death penalty completely.
The only real advocates of capital punishment are the police, who claim it is a deterrent to planned murders. In this regard, the death penalty certainly did not prevent the most infamous planned murder of our generation-the murder of President Kennedy. This was a murder carefully planned in advance and there is no evidence that there was any deterrent value at all in the fact that the state of Texas retains the death penalty.
In 1962, Ronald Turpin and Arthur Lucas were hanged in my own city of Toronto. The next night, in the shadow of the jail, a man was stabbed to death. As I have said, all the evidence indicates that the death penalty as a deterrent to murder is completely ineffective. Some have argued that it provides protection for the police. If this were so, there might be some reason for retaining it. The only comprehensive study made in this regard was conducted by the University of Pennsylvania. The chiefs of police of some 10,000 towns reported on cases of murder in which the victims were police officers, and an analysis showed no difference whatever between the positions of states which had

Criminal Code
retained the death penalty and states which had abolished it. Some police officers here claim that the existence of the death penalty for murder keeps criminals from moving into their jurisdictions. It seems to me that this contention cannot stand up, because if criminals in the United States wish to move into jurisdictions where there is no death penalty, they have six states of their own from which to choose. Others contend that the loved ones and relatives of a murdered person suffer and that the dependants of the murderer, the people left by him, should therefore suffer, too.
But surely, Mr. Speaker, the care and attention to be devoted to the families of those who are murdered can be better handled through compensation funds and other measures which could easily be devised. The final argument-and it may have some merit-is that public opinion is not prepared to support the abolition of capital punishment. In this regard it is significant that over the years the number of people in Canada who are in favour of retaining the death penalty is steadily declining. I believe the latest figures, taken in 1962, showed that only 47 per cent were still in favour of retaining it. Also it seems to me that in the area of social reforms it is highly necessary that our governments not just follow public opinion but lead it; that our governments should give leadership in areas of reform, rather than wait until a majority of the population want something and then turn around and agree with them.
I think the most important statement in this regard was made by Sir Ernest Gowers who served as chairman of the royal commission in the United Kingdom in 1949. He said as follows:
Before serving on the royal commission I, like most other people, had given no great thought to this problem. If I had been asked for my opinion, I should probably have said that I was in favour of the death penalty, and disposed to regard abolitionists as people whose hearts were bigger than their heads. Four years of close study on the subject gradually dispelled that feeling. In the end I became convinced that the abolitionists were right in their conclusions-and that so far from the sentimental approach leading into their camp and the rational one into that of the supporters, it was the other way about.
So I suggest that when one examines any of the arguments in favour of the retaining of capital punishment, they cannot stand up on any logical grounds.
My time is limited, Mr. Speaker, and I want to pass very quickly to the arguments in favour of abolition. The first argument, of course, in favour of abolishing the death penalty is that all arguments in favour of retaining it do not stand up unless we are prepared to admit that the real motive is revenge; and if that is the case, we have not
IMr. Scott.]
really progressed very far from the day when our ancestors dressed in leopard skins and chased each other around with clubs. The other argument against retaining capital punishment, of course, is the impossibility of rectifying a mistake, because the dead cannot come back to life. I know there are safeguards in our jurisprudence

we are all aware of them-but our jurisprudence is administered by human beings, not by calculating machines, and mistakes do occur and there are cases of innocent people being convicted. I have in my hands a book by Judge Jerome Frank in which he outlines some 36 cases of innocent people who were convicted. In the case of those who were executed, the interest in their case dies when they are executed because there is nobody to be released in any event. I spoke last session of the Coffin case. I do not intend to repeat here the arguments I advanced at that time, except to say that if ever there was a case that called for the abolition of capital punishment, it was the case of Wilbur Coffin. We shall await with great interest the deliberations of and the result and report of the royal commission.
Also, Mr. Speaker, capital punishment rules out any hope of rehabilitation of the criminal. Recent studies that have been conducted in forensic psychiatry have indicated that in many cases rehabilitation can take place. There is an interesting study of a young convict in Chicago who was convicted of murder and sentenced to death and whose execution was postponed for eight years. At the end of the eight years the governor of the state commuted his sentence to life imprisonment because this man had been completely rehabilitated. It was stated that to take his life would not be punishment but would only be retribution. As I have said, Mr. Speaker, capital punishment rules out any hope of rehabilitation. Life imprisonment, where it has been tried and where statistical evidence is available, has proven to be just as effective a deterrent as hanging in cases of murder.
It has been said by some that this has not been a particularly distinguished parliament. We have been subject to a great deal of criticism, some justified and some unjustified; but it seems to me that in this bill we have a chance to take a great step forward; to take action that would be heard around the world should we decide to take a forward and progressive step and abolish capital punishment.
Mr. Speaker, my time is running out and I do not really have an opportunity to go into the final problem of capital punishment, which is the whole question of morals and ethics; to what extent the state has the right to take a human life, under any circumstances. Every time we have a hanging in Canada, this country

undergoes a sort of crisis of conscience, where a man waits to die and the whole nation debates whether or not he shall die; and it usually resolves into a tug-of-war between the primitive passion of revenge and the civilized idea of compassion. We kill, I think, largely from revenge. I think we kill because we fear, not because we think these people are beyond rehabilitation. I think we kill in the blind and futile hope that others will not repeat the crime. I think we do it because we do not yet understand that murder has its roots in the ills of our society, poverty and ignorance, lack of opportunity and all the other ills with which we try to deal in this parliament. I think we do it because as yet we do not really respect human life.
The ministry of justice in Belgium-where their last execution was 100 years ago-put it this way:
The lesson has been learned that the best means of inculcating respect for human life is to refrain from taking it even in the name of the law.
I wonder to what extent a society that takes human life can invest its citizens with respect for human life. These, as I say, are arguments that would take a great deal of time to develop; they are matters of conscience. However, I hope that some day we shall have a chance to deal with them in this chamber. In summation, Mr. Speaker, I merely want to reaffirm that the arguments of the deterrent effect, protection of the police, etc., are not borne out by any available statistics that I can find; that the case in favour of the abolition of capital punishment has never been refuted on anything but opinion evidence; that as far as I can see, and on all the evidence, life imprisonment, where it has been tried, has exercised the necessary degree of effective deterrence.
Therefore in conclusion I merely wish again to reaffirm my position. It seems to me that the abolition of capital punishment is in many ways a plea that we put our backs to the past and try to turn our faces to the future. I think we are trying to establish a regard for human life that does not exist at the present time. I think we are trying, essentially, to argue for a time when reasons of revenge and hatred do not dictate our decisions, and for a time when we can learn .somehow through reason, judgment and understanding that all life is worth saving and that compassion is the highest attribute * of our society.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH CAPITAL PUNISHMENT EXCEPT FOR TREASON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the earliest days of civilization men have been concerned with capital punishment and its effects on the aggrieved
Criminal Code
person or persons, the criminal and the community as a whole. Today I become one of those who have given some thought to capital punishment and its social effects. Crime or criminology has only recently become a science of which we know much, or rather have studied as such.
In the days when Babylon was at the height of its prominence the generally recognized and accepted law was that in all criminal matters the maxim of "an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth" should prevail. Today such a rudimentary concept fills us, or should fill us, with alarm and yet as history, and supposedly civilization, advanced we find that this old maxim "an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth" has not only remained but has become worse. The Romans punished parricide by sewing the condemned in a sack with a dog, a cock, a viper and an ape and casting all into the sea or river. In eighth century England all laws made distinction between different classes of men, not only between slaves and free men but between different classes of free men, and all laws assumed that the family bore a share of responsibility for the wrongs done by its members and was entitled to some compensation for wrongs suffered by kinsmen.
In plain English the effect of the eighth century Anglo-Saxon procedure is this. A man accused of assaulting a fellow citizen needed the good opinion of the village to get off. If he had it, he would not be convicted; but if he committed his crime against the lord of the manor, then he only got off if he had sufficient testimony from the other local land owners. If the accused person persisted in his protestations of innocence and did not have the good opinion of his fellows, he had to submit to ordeal. The ordinary ordeals were by water or fire-a hot iron weighing one pound had to be carried, or the arm plunged up to the wrist in boiling water. For a threefold ordeal the weight of the iron was three pounds, or the arm had to be put in up to the elbow. The hand was then bound and sealed up and kept bound for three days. If, after three days, the hand showed raw flesh the man was guilty. If the hand healed he was innocent.
These ordeals were accepted by eighth century England. It is reported a great number of convictions were obtained, almost as many convictions perhaps as would have been the case under the proposed bill no. 99 in the Ontario legislature, whereby accused people would be denied legal counsel, habeas corpus would be removed, Magna Carta done away with, and people put in jail for days on end and kept there if they failed to answer

Criminal Code
questions. It has been said that this bill no. 99 would apply only to selected persons, but I hate to think who the selected persons might be. I do not know whether they would have been Liberals first of all or who they might have been, but being a little bit selective is a dangerous thing, like a little bit of something else which I am sure the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) is thinking about now.
