speechtext:
Fortunately bill no. 99 was K.O'd. in the second round. Cassius Clay, the world heavyweight champion, took seven rounds to win the championship, but it just goes to show that many a Cassius has feet of clay-and here I am referring to the proposed bill no. 99.
Then 900 years later in the 17th century in England we might logically suppose that men were much more enlightened than their forebears of the eighth century. Yet we find that in 1650 an act was passed in England punishing adultery with death, and this savage penalty was actually inflicted in two or three cases. After that even puritan juries refused to convict and the law was set aside as unworkable. This was rather remarkable, in that history shows us that it usually take a long time for legislatures to change a criminal law which is not supported, nay is even despised, by the majority of the people.
People in the seventeenth century or in the eighth century were no less intelligent than people of the twentieth century. Rather, the power of traditional thought was very effective in keeping men's minds closed to the facts which were not in accordance with traditions. Previous to the time of William Harvey, whose work was done early in the seventeenth century, the ablest and most intelligent persons had no proper concept of the circulation of the blood. They believed the arteries were filled with air. Harvey's findings gained very little headway during his lifetime and were contradicted most strenuously by scientific men. This was due again in a large part to that tradition of thought of which I have spoken.
It is not my intention to be maudlin in describing the various tortures and punishments inflicted in England, but I feel that we must look at these punishments in order to grasp the change in men's thinking. Of course, when I say men I mean both sexes, and it may be that a large credit for the reforms that have been made are due to the influence and innate gentleness of the female sex.
In 1530 an act was passed in England which prescribed boiling alive for certain convicted persons. Burning alive was another penalty

for a certain number of crimes and lasted until 1790, only 174 years ago. From 1525 until 1550 it is said 72,000 executions were performed in England. Nevertheless crime increased and during the eighteenth century the criminal code of England contained 240 different capital offences. At the dawn of the last century death was a penalty for such misdemeanours as unlawfully killing, hunting or stealing deer, unlawfully killing or netting fish out of any pond, cutting down or destroying someone else's trees, sending threatening letters; and, of course, thefts of over five shillings from a shop or over 40 shillings from a private house were also punishable by death.
From time to time men have protested against these outrages. One such person was Cesare di Beccaria, a Milanese nobleman whose book "Crimes and Punishment" published in 1764 denounced torture and established a basis for a scientific treatment of criminology. This book was a tremendous sensation among enlightened people all over Europe. However, Beccaria was denounced by his critics-and they were many-as a fanatic, an impostor, a fool, a madman, and was charged with having sought to endanger governments and seduce the public; while torture was upheld by these critics as a benefit and a mercy to a criminal by purging him in his death of falsehood.
Due to the efforts of such men as Beccaria, we have in Canada at the present time but three offences punishable by death. They are treason, murder and piracy with violence. However, let us look at and study carefully the death penalty. It can be attacked on several grounds. I propose to deal with it on the grounds that it fulfils no useful function and that it will be remembered by future generations with a sense of loathing and incredulity. The argument is put forth that fear of the death penalty is a major deterring influence on the crime of murder. Yet in those countries and states which have abolished the death penalty for murder there has been no increase in the crime. My hon. friend from Danforth (Mr. Scott) gave a very learned discourse a few moments ago in this house on this very matter. Neither has there been a lessening of this particular crime. The only logical conclusion at which we can arrive is that fear of the death penalty is no effective deterrent.
It is also argued that it prevents the repetition of the same crime by the same person. I shall quote the late Warden Lewis E. Lawes of Sing Sing prison. These extracts from his book "Life and Death in Sing Sing".
The argument that capital punishment is necessary for elimination of murder is faulty: It must

not be forgotten that the death penalty has been tried before on a colossal scale, judged and found wanting.
The further assumption that the murderer is a dangerous criminal from whom society must be protected by hanging or capital punishment is flatly disproved by the figures which show that 90 per cent of the men and women convicted for murder had no previous felony record whatsoever.
Finally Warden Lawes asks this question:
Is it necessary to kill a murderer? It is surely not a deterrent example to perform an act furtively. If the state really believes that execution is necessary to deter others, it should execute openly and unashamed. Does not this furtiveness carry the suggestive thought that the spectacle of legalized killing by the state breeds on the part of the unthinking mass a hardened outlook towards murder which is harmful rather than effective as a deterrent?
It may very well be that my thoughts and feelings toward capital punishment are not shared by the majority of Canadians who approve of capital punishment and believe it is right. That a thing is widely believed is no guarantee of its truth. For a much longer time than the present view has prevailed, it was universally believed that the sun moved around the earth; the whole world believed in the existence of witches, and up until the time of Columbus the prevalent belief was that the world was flat. Therefore the fact that belief in the desirability of capital punishment is both widespread and of long standing is not by itself a guarantee that it is the true solution. We have seen that savage punishments have neither reformed the criminal class nor acted as a deterrent for the future.
There was something which was brought to my attention yesterday that might be of interest to this house. It was a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada which voted on a split decision, if I may put it that way, that an accused person from Quebec, who had been condemned to death at his original trial and who subsequently had his execution sentence set aside by the court of appeal of the province of Quebec which ordered a new trial, be now executed, and that the decision of the Quebec appeal court be set aside. This was by a majority decision of six to three in the Supreme Court of Canada.
I submit that when there is, for whatever reason, anything less than a unanimous vote in a court of appeal or in the Supreme Court of Canada on a matter affecting a man's life, that man should not be executed and instead should at least be sentenced to life imprisonment. I ask the government to take note of this in any amendments that may be proposed to the Criminal Code.
I believe that the legislation enacted some three years ago was a step in the right direction, providing for two classes of murder, capital and non-capital. We have had three
Criminal Code
years experience of that legislation and, so far as it goes, it has worked very well. However, I would ask that the government study this very carefully over the next year or two in the hope that it will then say there will not be two classes of murder, that there will be only non-capital murder, and that the penalty will be life imprisonment, as suggested in this very excellent bill presented by the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott).

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH CAPITAL PUNISHMENT EXCEPT FOR TREASON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although I am not a lawyer or a legislator, I am nevertheless interested in this matter and I should like to say, to begin on a humourous note, that capital punishment should be abolished, at least in the case of bills presented during the hour for the consideration of private members' business, thus permitting us to adopt some of them once in a while.
I suggest we proceed most cautiously regarding abolishment of capital punishment and that we consider seriously every reason invoked in favour of it.
I agree that capital punishment may not be the deterrent we think it is, that it does not constitute a protection for police officers and that it cannot become an instrument of revenge against an individual. I admit that we must provide some social reforms, one of which would be the abolition of capital punishment.
Besides when it has become an accomplished fact, there will still be cases where, for the public safety-and not necessarily that of the policemen since it is their job just as it is the firemen's job to put our fires, even at the risk of getting burned-we will have to find more adequate means of protecting the people.
I still recall that famous case to which I have often referred here-and you could even say that I am obsessed by the idea- that of Dion who was sentenced to several years in the penitentiary and while the judge recommended that he should not be allowed to leave it for reasons which are still unknown, in spite of the numerous questions directed to the Minister of Justice, Dion managed to be released legally through the parole board. Once free, he lost no time in committing murders.
That is what I have in mind when I say that the law must still be made to protect the people. If someone is sentenced to jail for life, there is nothing to prevent him, after ten, 20 or 25 years of perfectly good behaviour, from being paroled, returning to live in society and committing another murder.
It is claimed that we have no right to deprive somebody of his life. But, before a

Criminal Code
murderer is sentenced to death, would it not be more logical to give an accurate definition of a real murderer, a killer capable of committing a premeditated murder, and a sick person suffering from mental illness. In my opinion, mentally unbalanced people should not be given a death sentence. They should be treated, or at least some kind of treatment should be tried in their case. On the other hand, life sentences are not given those who are capable of deliberately committing a premeditated murder, in order to enable our laws, not to satisfy any desire for revenge, but to ensure the protection of our people who can always expect to see that individual come out again.
As a deterrent, it has been alleged that a life sentence is similar to a death sentence, except that, in the latter case, the individual will never have any chance of returning to society.
Mistrials have also been mentioned, but they are certainly not a result of death sentences, but rather of loop-holes in our laws. Now, I think that legal means should be taken in order to avoid any possible mistakes. But there is definitely no relationship between capital punishment and mistrials.
In those very few cases, those convicted as a result of a mistrial, as the hon. member for Hastings South (Mr. Temple) pointed out, should be convicted only on complete unanimity. I maintain that when both lawyers and psychiatrists are unanimous in finding someone guilty of premeditated murder, with full knowledge of the facts, capital punishment should be maintained in order to protect the people.
Earlier, the hon. member for Hastings South said that many things have changed since the early days when it was said: "an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth". In that respect we know-and I recall it especially since it is Holy Week.-that when our Saviour came among us, He said: from now on, it will not be "an eye for an eye or a tooth for a tooth" but "whosoever smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also" which means that we have to forgive one another and live by charity and love only. He said that we must forgive often, that we must forgive seventy times seven, meaning that we must always forgive one another. But, just the same-He even let himself be sentenced to death following a charge, a political trial, in short for various reasons which, in our opinion, did not warrant the death penalty. But he accepted that fate to show that, in future, capital punishment could be contemplated in some cases; otherwise, I feel He would have refused it himself.

Before ending my remarks, I would like to add that the hon. member for Hastings South says that something is not necessarily true because most people accept it. We have been saying that for a long time too, we have been saying that the present economic system is not good but, in spite of that, everyone still thinks that it cannot be changed. It is still a good argument.
We favour the abolishment of the death penalty, but until it can be established without any possible doubt that an accused was not entirely sound of mind or that he had not fully premeditated his murder, I feel we must leave in the criminal code a provision to protect the public against true criminals.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH CAPITAL PUNISHMENT EXCEPT FOR TREASON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question raised in Bill C-12 with respect to capital punishment is certainly a much debated one throughout Canada.
Some people claim that capital punishment must be maintained and others state that it should be abolished.
Moreover, if we consider section 75, paragraph 1 of this bill, we see that there is not much change as compared to what existed previously.
I quote:
(1)	Everyone commits piracy who does any act that, by the law of nations, is piracy.
Now, what is suggested in Bill C-12 is exactly the same thing as in this paragraph 1.
But it is paragraph (2) that this bill would change, and paragraph (2) read previously as follows:
(2)	Everyone who commits piracy while in or out of Canada is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for life, but if while committing or attempting to commit piracy he murders or attempts to murder another person or does any act that is likely to endanger the life of another person he shall be sentenced to death.
Now, the new section, paragraph (2) says:
Everyone who commits piracy while in or out of Canada is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for life.
In the explanatory notes, this is specified:
The purpose of this bill is to provide that hereafter a person shall not, except in certain cases of treason, be sentenced in Canada to suffer death for murder but that such a person shall hereafter be liable to imprisonment for life.
Now, what does Bill C-12 mean by:
"except in certain cases of treason"?
For instance, is it not treason for an individual to disguise as Santa Claus and kill two policemen in the very centre of the city of Montreal at noontime? Is it not treason to deprive children of their father and a wife of her husband? In the case of sure premeditation-because the bandit is then ready

for any eventuality-is it not treason of the Canadian community where this individual may live?
The first part of the explanatory notes reads as follows:
The 1960-61 act to be repealed has the effect of dividing murder into two kinds, capital and non-capital; and of providing death as punishment for capital murder and imprisonment for life in the case of non-capital murder.
Mr. Speaker, when it is clearly established that the murderer knew full well the seriousness of his act, I feel that he should pay with his own life for the one he has taken.
On the other hand, miscarriages of justice have been known to happen. For instance, an investigation is going on at present in the province of Quebec concerning a well-publicized case, that of Wilbert Coffin who was executed in 1956, after two or three trials and after three years of detention in jail.
And today they are trying to find reasons to exonerate or rather rehabilitate the memory of Wilbert Coffin.
Mr. Speaker, I think that the Coffin case was not clear in 1956, and many jurists readily admit it. There was no conclusive evidence that he was the murderer of the three American tourists in the Gaspe peninsula. This was not, in my opinion, a capital murder, and I feel the criminal code should be amended so as to prevent such a miscarriage of justice.
It may be that Coffin was guilty, but then maybe he was not. In such cases, the accused should be given the benefit of the doubt and not be sentenced to death. I feel that the majority of Canadians would welcome such an amendment to the Criminal Code.
But, Mr. Speaker, throughout the country, there are criminals who do not hesitate to fire on policemen, on fathers and mothers of families, on taxi drivers to steal money from them.
These days we hear more and more about hold ups. As a matter of fact, it was even said that there had been a hold up every minute in the city of Montreal recently during almost a whole night. Those are the hold ups that are reported. What about those which are not?
I feel that there must be a way to improve the situation, and it is not by reducing sentences that we will prevent people from stealing or engaging in hold ups or having the nerve, the audacity to kill anyone they find in their way.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Hastings South (Mr. Temple) pointed out to the house a short while ago that we no longer live in the middle ages or in ancient or primitive times.
Criminal Code
But, even if we are living in modern times, we must be cautious and know where we are going before proposing the abolishment of a punishment which in certain cases certainly proves to be the best.
When we see people die in such a way, even friends in certain cases, I can assure you this makes one think twice about the advisability of abolishing capital punishment.
Mr. Speaker, this bill and other similar ones have been introduced here for a number of sessions. Life sentence has been suggested rather than capital punishment. To deprive someone of freedom for a lifetime, I wonder whether it is more Christian and more modern than to punish him according to what he deserves, according to the seriousness of the act he committed.
We consider only whether a murder is capital or non-capital to determine exactly if capital punishment should be maintained or not. I feel that capital punishment should be maintained for capital murders. In addition, as suggested earlier by the hon. member for Hastings South, legal proceedings should be more thorough so as to establish exactly the seriousness of the offence committed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH CAPITAL PUNISHMENT EXCEPT FOR TREASON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) is to be commended for bringing this important matter to the attention of parliament again. The reason I have risen to speak in this debate is that I have taken part in previous discussions of this subject, notably on the several successive bills which were presented and moved in the house between 1958 and 1962 by the former member for York-Scarborough, Mr. Frank McGee. I spoke on those occasions and I propose to speak now in support of the principle of abolition of capital punishment. After each occasion in the past when I expressed my views against capital punishment I received letters from my constituents and others both for and against the retention of the death sentence, with the number favouring abolition on the increase over previous years.
Undoubtedly, the general feeling swaying toward abolition had the effect of influencing the previous government in the introduction of Bill No. C-92 in May of 1961, the passing of which had the effect of dividing murder into capital and non-capital categories. I think this was a step in the right direction.
The Globe and Mail devoted an editorial to commenting on the passage of Bill No. C-92 in 1961, and concluded with these words:
The new amendment will reduce the number of cases in which the government is required to exact the extreme penalty or to interfere with the law,

Criminal Code
but they do not answer the moral question: Should society kill any man, whatever his or her crime?
This issue, however, is still between two schools of thought, one thirsting after justice in a mood of vengeance and the other urging the practice of Christian charity and the rehabilitation of criminals. Mr. Kirkpatrick, an executive director of the John Howard Society for Ontario, speaking on deterrence, had this to say:
The belief behind deterrent punishment is that behaviour can be controlled by fear; therefore, the argument goes, severe treatment of a criminal is effective in two directions at once: It deters the criminal himself from committing another crime and, by the example of his punishment, it deters others from wrongdoing.
Notable figures in the religious life of this country have gone on record as being in favour of abolition, Still others have expressed opinions to the contrary, holding to the belief that fear of the death sentence is a restraining force against murder. Personally, I share the views of those who believe that there is no valid guarantee that the fear of punishment by death is a definite deterrent.
Consider the proportion of murders committed in circumstances of sudden passion which are not deterred by threat of consequences and consider also crime such as robberies, from which murder might result, which are deliberately planned to avoid detection. Consider also the risk of executing an innocent person.
May I cite as an example the case of a man by the name of Evans, who was hanged in London for the murder of his wife and child in 1949. Five years later a man by the name of Christie, who lived in an apartment in the same house as Evans, was arrested and convicted of having murdered several women including Mrs. Evans, for whose murder her husband was hanged five years before. Consider the case now under investigation known as the Coffin case in the province of Quebec. There are others that could be cited.
The debates on capital punishment during 1959, 1960 and 1961 revealed the tremendous interest in this subject which the whole country shared. It was a practical demonstration of the feelings of the people on the matter which were, for the most part, still divided. Those who still favour the retention of the death penalty for crimes involving murder believe that death is the only effective deterrent against murder. While I respect the views of those who hold the opinion that the death sentence is a restraining force against murder, the experience of nations,

including the United States to the south of us, is such that it does not bear out this contention.
The hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) mentioned some of the nations that have abolished capital punishment. I could add Belgium to that list, which abolished capital punishment in 1863; Luxembourg in 1822; Portugal in 1867; the Netherlands in 1870 and Italy in 1890. The death penalty was restored in Italy during the fascist regime but was abolished again in 1948. The northern states south of the border might also be included, and this is not a complete list by any means.
I should like now, Mr. Speaker, to read an extract from the report of the royal commission on capital punishment in Great Britain in 1949. At page 53 of the report the commission said:
Capital punishment has obviously failed as a deterrent when murder is committed. We can number its failures. But we cannot number its successes. No one can ever know how many people have refrained from murder because of the fear of being hanged. For that we have to rely on indirect and inconclusive evidence. We have been told that the first thing a murderer says when he is arrested is often, "shall I be hanged" or, "I did it and I am ready to swing for it" or something of that kind. What is the inference to be drawn from this? Clearly not that the death penalty is an effective deterrent, for he has not been deterred; nor that he consciously considered the risk of the death penalty and accepted it; still less that the death penalty was not so effective a deterrent as some other punishment might have been. The true inference seems to us to be that there is a strong association between murder and the death penalty in the popular imagination.
I see that the time is getting short, but I should like to say that I do not propose that the government should bring in a bill to a divided parliament, on a subject about which there is divided opinion in the country. I am in favour of letting this question come to a free vote eventually, and letting every member vote according to the dictates of his or her conscience.

The Budget-Mr. Diefenbaker statement when he spoke of what had taken place in the house, which I am not doing-I am telling what took place on the outside- and he said, "if terminological inexactitude is parliamentary I certainly substitute it with the greatest of pleasure."

He spoke with pride of the degree of prosperity in the economy. Then with that modesty which characterizes him at all times he said: Here I am; I brought this about. What have they done? What have they produced? I listened today with interest to ascertain what had been brought about. What policies have they inaugurated? What brought about the rising economy in this country such as we predicted would happen? I am going to quote from these two documents which are entirely free of any suggestion of partisanship. I mentioned devaluation a moment ago; I also referred to the import surcharges and to wheat sales, each and every one of them our policies. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Watson) produced a package of wheat and I can only say when I think of some of the statements made by hon. gentlemen opposite that it is too bad he was not here earlier so that they would have been able to see what wheat was like. They said there was nothing more dangerous than selling wheat to communist countries. They said: This is a terrible thing; this is something we would never countenance. Devaluation? Never under any circumstances. Let me point out that as far as devaluation is concerned the following appears on page 8 of the Bank of Canada report:
One development that has contributed a great deal to the Canadian economy's performance in recent years has been the improvement in Canada's international competitive position. This was greatly strengthened by the decline in the foreign exchange value of the Canadian dollar in 1960-62-
I refer now to page 47 of the white paper, and I quote this as an answer to the so-called arguments advanced today by the minister as he delivered what seemed to me to be his swan song. On page 47 the white paper says:
The trend of imports in the current upswing has been affected by a number of factors, including the devaluation of the Canadian dollar, the temporary import surcharges, the pattern of demand, and changes in the structure of the Canadian

The measures taken in the middle of 1962 to deal with the foreign exchange emergency resulted in a sharp reduction in the current account deficit-
I am simply putting these quotations on the record without observation. They need no interpretation. Again, the minister boasted today of the improvement in the payments position. More than half of this improvement can be attributed to the unusual wheat and flour sales to the Soviet union.
I say that if it had not been for the former government selling wheat to communist nations, wheat would never have been sold to the U.S.S.R. With that naivete characteristic of the minister-

I hope "naivete" is not going to jar the sensibilities of the people opposite who interrupt. The minister said we had a crisis in foreign exchange. Does he forget that the Liberal government had a crisis in foreign exchange in 1947? Does he forget that? Has he forgotten that he had one last July which he concealed from the Canadian people until it was revealed in the Bank of Canada report? He did not talk about these things today. How was the last potential crisis, the one that the government concealed from parliament, met? The Bank of Canada report says on page 6:
The announcement in mid-September of exceptionally large export sales of wheat and flour to the Soviet union dispelled immediate concern about the possibility of renewed foreign exchange difficulties for Canada-
I emphasize the word "immediate". In other words, we are not out of the woods yet. The concern is dispelled, provided there is an inflow of investment capital into Canada, and I intend to deal with that. I have already referred to devaluation and I do not want to put any more quotations on the record. I simply say that the Liberals went across Canada and they deceived the people, and I emphasize the word "deceived". Just read the record. I am not talking about them deceiving now; they have become paragons of all perfection and I would be the last to say anything in this house to indicate that they would have that characteristic today. But they told

the Canadian people that devaluation was dangerous. What does the Bank of Canada report say on page 51?
-the devaluation of the Canadian dollar improved the competitive position of Canadian industry.
Sir, it is difficult to understand why a political party would have endeavoured to undermine the Canadian economy by statements which have subsequently been proven to be untrue by the very fact that what they condemned they now adhere to.
What about the next step? What about American investment? There the tinkerers really worked. Do you recall how they said we were anti-American? They said we brought about a dialogue. Oh, it has been a wonderful change that has taken place. We go to Washington and we find out what the situation is there. We have the solution now for these problems. Then after having the Hyannis Port meeting the very first thing that happens is that the Minister of Finance proceeds to place before parliament a 30 per cent tax in order to interfere with the movement of capital between our country and the United States. He had to withdraw it. Then he added 5 per cent to the withholding tax, and what happened? The serious financial position in Canada today is only controlled to a reasonable degree by the fact that sales of wheat to communist countries have taken place. In the present budget there is a watered down version. What happened when the policies of the amateur economists who write books were carried into effect? What happened? The Bank of Canada report says that the rate of inflows, that is of United States capital, fell sharply after mid-year.
Page 52 of this report reads in part as follows:
These Inflows which exceeded $1,300 million in 1956 and 1957, were reduced to $584 million in 1963.
What do we find? The inflow for the first three months was some $140 million; for the next three months, $390 million and for the third three months, that is the period from July to September, it fell to $98 million. We have not had a report as yet for the last three months, although computations show that the amount coming into Canada instead of being $390 million is down to about $65 million. Why did the minister not tell us something about that this afternoon? What is he going to do about it? There is no answer at all. I had to refer to these matters, sir, because of the fact the hon. gentleman attributed the advance in our economy to the actions of this government and refused to admit that these policies which today receive a eulogy

in the Bank of Canada report, and also in the white paper, were policies introduced by us.

Yes, doubled, trebled and quadrupled as the hon. member says. I admire the conservative attitude of the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan). They said we were selling for credit to our enemies and taking cash from our friends for wheat. Well, we provided credits.
The Budget-Mr. Diefenbaker
The next thing is industrial policies. We introduced policies to encourage in Canada, by incentive but not by domination, the extension of industry within our country.
What about defence sharing? Under our government defence sharing mounted greatly in Canada for the first time since 1953 and, for the first time, we had a reasonable share of defence expenditures from the United States. Then, the report says that the temporary import surcharges which were still in effect in the early months of 1963 have also contributed to the change.
Now, sir, I have had to point these things out. I do not like to go over the record like this, but the hon. gentleman insisted that it should be done. What about the present situation? What is going to be done in order to ensure that Canada shall receive her reasonable share of United States investment? I can only point out what the white paper says, and that is that uncertainty continued to prevail in Canadian financial markets. There was virtually no Canadian borrowing in the United States from mid-July until the present time. Why was this? It resulted from the fact these people over there undermined confidence in Canada, and showed foreign investors that they could no longer rely on the integrity of Canadian promises.
I should like also to point out a reference I made earlier, and I would not do this if I had not been dragged into the debate. The Minister of Finance made a statement that we had a financial crisis. I ask him why he has not explained the situation in Canada. Why did he not explain what took place last July and August when they had a similarly threatening situation which was met temporarily by the fact that wheat sales to Russia provided foreign exchange? As I listened today to the hon. gentleman reveal what the present government has done, I noted one of the things he particularly underlined was what had been done to employ men and women over 45 years of age. All I can say in that connection is that the total number is 1,000. There are more than 12,000 over 65, and we do not know how many there are between 45 and 65. The cost was fabulous-that is, the cost of advertising. This is another example of the wasteful attitude of this government in spending hundreds of thousands of dollars on advertising in politically friendly advertising companies.
I am going to turn to the next phase. What about dominion-provincial relations? I see the genial Minister of Justice (Mr. Fa-vreau) here. If I had time I should like to analyse the speech he made last evening. There is one thing you can say about him, and that is he is consistent. It was a great

The Budget-Mr. Diefenbaker speech, according to the reports, but it did not get down to any particular. He predicted that a divorce was possible between the provincial Liberal party and the federal Liberal party in the province of Quebec. At least, there would be a parliamentary separation, but there was nothing to indicate what the attitude of the government was going to be on dominion-provincial relations.
This budget offers no hope to the provinces. Where are the items in this budget which will place flesh and blood on the bones of promise? They have set up the skeleton. They said they were going to help out the provinces. What do they intend to do? What is the plan? As a matter of fact I think the present budget, together with the fact that the minister went no further today than he did, indicates that this government, contrary to its pledged word, intends to do nothing other than play around with the question of joint programs. It does not intend to carry out its promise that the provinces will be enabled to have the necessary moneys with which to discharge their responsibilities. In the terms of the present budget I see a calculated and callous affront to the provinces.
I turn, now, to another subject-the attitude taken in connection with the Eskimos. I want to refer to that. The Eskimos are our responsibility under the law and under the constitution. I believe the minister of northern affairs (Mr. Laing) feels very keenly on this subject. But some of the other ministers in the cabinet seem to regard the Eskimo as tradable, as expendable. To carry out the present policy of disposing of them in the absence of a constitutional amendment would not only be unjust and unfair but would make a travesty of the constitution of this country. We do not intend to have the Eskimos, these people who are our responsibility, bartered as chattels or sublet for the sake of political expediency. I do not enter into provincial matters, but I say this: These Eskimos will not be placed in Mr. Levesque's hands just because Mr. Levesque wants them there. More will be said of this, because we in this country have a responsibility towards these people and, again, I emphasize that they cannot be removed from the jurisdiction under whose authority they are constitutionally placed merely by a simple agreement made between the federal government and a provincial government.
I heard nothing in the speech today about that banner with the device "Canadianization of Industry". Canadianization; we heard so much about that. It was in the book. It was also in the report. I will say this to the minister-that the report was one which showed a great deal of work applied to a very large problem. But nothing was said about this

Canadianization today. Nothing. Just uncertainty. I ask the minister in connection with Canadianization: Why did he evacuate the Canada development plan? Why did he desert that great principle? Who interfered? Who made it impossible for the hon. gentleman to carry it out? He had the vim. He had the vision of which he spoke. It turned out to be a nightmare. What happened to the Canada development corporation?
He pictured today what was going to happen

the development of the Columbia; the development of the Nelson river. All I can tell the hon. gentleman in this connection is that he was a little wrong in his history this afternoon when he said it was only under the present government that arrangements had been made to ship outside Canada power surplus to our needs. We brought that into effect in 1962. Yet, this afternoon, in a characteristic manner, an attempt was made to appropriate to the party opposite a policy which hon. members sitting over there criticized in the years from 1957 to 1961.
What about the Nelson river? We set up a full investigation into the potentialities of that development and, having arrived at an alteration in our policy with regard to the export of power, there are hopes that it will be proceeded with. Mention was made of the great potential in Labrador and I join with the hon. minister in expressing the hope that this development will be proceeded with at the earliest possible moment to the end that we shall be producing this power in Canada which, a few years hence, may not be as important as it is today if the cost of atomic energy becomes reasonably close to that of power produced by water.
What about the magazine situation? Canadianization? The resolutions are on the order paper; I may not refer to them now. But I must say there are many people in Canada today whose opinion is changing in this regard. They are asking themselves this question-whether or not Time and Reader's Digest should be absolved from the general legislative enactment respecting United States magazines and other foreign magazines which are brought into Canada particularly for advertising purposes.
Within the last few days an editorial has appeared in the Montreal Star which is of interest in this connection. It points out this:
These two magazines now dump their product into Canada after a manner and in a fashion which would not be tolerated by any government which seeks to prevent unfair competition from foreign producers If it was china or tinware, if it was boots and shoes, if it was shirtwaists or any other form of textiles, the government would have moved in, horse, foot and artillery, to stop the imports. But these two magazines import into this country their whole editorial content, collected at a cost greatly exceeding the budget available

to any Canadian magazine, and use it as the bait to attract advertising which might otherwise be available to a genuine Canadian magazine.
The article goes on to ask what the hon. members who represent Montreal constituencies are doing about this. What of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Turner)? What about the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury)? Why has none of these men made any move to help the Canadian magazines? It goes on:
Mr. Drury, it may be noted, is very pleased with a scheme which he presented to the House of Commons to increase the Canadian content of the motorcar produced in Canada. He appears to be wholly uninterested in the Canadian magazine, a somewhat curious performance-
I say, Mr. Speaker, that more and more people are asking today, as they look at these magazines, why they should be placed in an exempted position. Views in this regard are not frozen. They could be changed with changing conditions. I simply point out that nothing has been done by this government which in any way indicates that the great policy of Canadianization will go far enough to ensure that Canadians will have the opportunity within their own land to have their own magazines, unchallenged by unjust competition from outside this country.
I simply throw that out, Mr. Speaker, and add that those views more and more are being expressed as Canadians realize the import of some things that are taking place within this nation.
Mr. Speaker, I am asking support for our amendment. The minister has asked, "How could you bring about a reduction in taxes, with a large deficit?" President Johnson of the United States has given lead in this regard; he has given the lead by reducing unnecessary expenditures. We, in 1962, cut off some $200 million.

I do not like to point out the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets) or anyone else, but the Minister of Public Works might be all for it in some other department; even the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp), or the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), with the tremendous expansion in the expenditures for foreign affairs-

speechtext:
-and all these other things. In the United States, instead of raising members' salaries, congress turned it down; they said, "We are not going to increase our salaries so long as we have taxation at its present level". What about 20220-91
The Budget-Mr. Latulippe Canada? Under this government everybody is getting an increase; fabulous increases are being granted. I think of the co-ordinator; I think that is the title of Mr. Kent. He brings together all these jarring elements; he brings about order out of chaos, and agreement in a cabinet that cannot agree. That is his job; he is worth $25,000 a year. But he has not done very well at it. They have been raising salaries all along the line, and the minister said that taxation in Canada is lower than that in the United States. I just want to say to him that he is the only one who has that view. Every responsible financial person in Canada has said, "What kind of blinkers was the minister wearing when he made that statement?" Our taxation today is higher than in the United States; it has increased, since this government came into power, by $390 million a year.
This afternoon the minister said, "Oh, the sales tax did not have any influence. We have the largest expenditures for investment in the first three months of this year". All I have to point out in that connection is that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture says the 11 per cent sales tax should be removed from production machinery used in agriculture. Every business across Canada has said that it should be removed, and that one of the major reasons for the increase in the last three months is the fact that they have been stockpiling against the increase from 4 per cent to 8 per cent and ultimately to 11 per cent. The minister produces the testimony of one man who said, in effect, "Great is Diana of the Ephesians".
Mr. Speaker, they said they would cut expenditures. What they have done is increase expenditures to a point far and beyond those ever before in effect in peacetime, except possibly during the Korean war. These are the people who were saying last year and the year before, "Just give us the opportunity and we will show you what we will do". They have, and the Canadian people today have no confidence in the government sitting opposite.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks, I should like to say that we disapprove the Conservative amendment because it is negative in every respect.
During their term of office, the Conservatives themselves did nothing but increase taxes and accumulate budget deficits.
The two old parties are in the same old boat. The more things change, the more they remain the same. Neither party had the

The Budget-Mr. Latulippe courage to go to the very root of the present trouble by changing the old system for a new one adapted to the year 1964.
In the process of adjusting themselves to modernization, progress, science and reforms, the two old parties prefer submissiveness to freedom from the financial dictatorship which smothers and strangles the people. That is why we refuse to support the amendment.
Neither party has found a solution to the present problems of debts, taxes, budget deficits and rises in the cost of living index which cause even more serious stagnation in Canada.
Our democratic system and our financial system are no longer compatible. Instead of living in a democracy, we have a genuine dictatorship which prevents the young, the aged, women and men from leading a life of their own choice. As I say, we are truly living under a dictatorship which exercises its control through hunger.
The present system indebted Canada to the tune of $75 million at the time of confederation. Today, after 96 years of labour and development, the national debt totals $25 billion.
The public debt is made up of money which is non-existent, which has never been issued and which the government has pledged itself to reimburse; the financier creates the money and lends it, but on the promise that all that money, which he has never earned, will be reimbursed to him with interest.
The banker alone creates modern money; he does not make capital, but he asks to be paid, besides the capital, interest which he does not make and which nobody makes. As money does not grow by itself, the swelling claimed ends up in the public debt. That is why the public debt is rising.
Our economy is infected. This method of creating money and lending it with interest right away is the most effective invention which was ever inspired by Satan in a human brain so as to bring havoc to the economy, scuttle the Ten Commandments, sow dissension and hate, change man into wolf towards his brothers and make him the slave of money.
It is the opening of the race for money, for the dollar, to avoid being the one who falls, even if it involves causing the fall of others. Money has become the motivation, the end of everything; instead of producing wheat to feed, clothes to clothe, shoes to shod, houses to house, we do all that to raise more money than was invested. It is a must. The financier is there watching, claiming the dollar he brought into the world and demanding a return, this thing that we must take from our neighbour since it has not been put beside the dollar lent. And so, the economic life

which has become horrible, hard, implacable and cruel, according to the words used by the Pope himself. How can we talk of charity, of unselfishness, of compassion when an unrelenting rule is hung over our heads which compels us, unless we want to starve with our family, to play the game to extract from our country more dollars than have been issued?
To claim interest on the new dollar, to issue in this way taxing money every time the development of the country requires an increase in money, that is equivalent to accepting a thief in the economy of the country, thanks to the progress and the development of the country; that is why progress hardens the life it should relieve. It is a mortgaged and, often, a foreclosed progress.
Everybody's life revolves around the dollar. The fertility imposed on money by the manufacturer of dollars kills the fertility of talent, of genius, of development itself. As for the government, it is known that all its activities are determined by the presence or the absence of dollars.
There is a technique to create money in this way and put it into circulation for the benefit of all, without doing any wrong to anybody: it is the Social Credit technique. It is money to the service of man instead of man to the service of money. No inflation and no deflation, but a balance between services. It is a philosophy quite different from the present scarce money banking philosophy.
Through an autonomous procedure, balance would be established and maintained, because it is the responsible power itself which would control the means to increase the active money supply, as it would also control the means to put in on a sounder basis as required.
How many unnecessary hardships were forced upon the world for the past 25 years because the last war was not financed with other interest-free money or money issued without interest.
The situation in Canada is a striking one. Our federal debt was $2,574,531,033 in 1919, while today, the gross debt is $24,799,139,867 and the net debt $13,919,769,972. On the other hand, since 1914, we paid $14,869,164,125 in interests only, which is more than the whole net debt at this time. This means that, if all interest charges had been eliminated, Canada would practically be without debts.
We are told time and again that it is impossible for the government to borrow money without having to pay interest. Now, who is above the government to lay down what it should do?
There are 265 members sitting in Ottawa, but, except among the members of the Social Credit party, not a single voice was raised

to mention these things and to conclude that, work demands money, and money requires borrowing, and if you want to borrow, you have to incur debts, which means that in order to develop this country, the public debt must increase in proportion. That is what the federal, provincial and municipal governments, the school boards and individuals are doing now.
Hon. members of the government, like your predecessors, you are gallantly fighting and struggling but you do not dare change the rules. You prefer to fold your hands and piously ask Canadians to make sacrifices by increasing direct and indirect taxes, by raising general taxation and therefore the cost of living. Rather than show disrespect to the bookkeepers, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) prefers to follow that course. To balance two columns in a book is much more important than the life of 2,900,000 heads of families, who have to support 12,400,000 persons, on small single people's salaries. To tighten the consumer's belt throughout the country in the presence of goods which accumulate, go bad or are destroyed, that is one of the administrative virtues of the present government.
Science and progress teach people to set their eyes on realities. Now, this diabolic system does not satisfy young people, their aspirations or their ideals; they do not want to live in unemployment, to rob Peter to allow Paul to exist, even if this alleged liberty confers the right to cast a vote into the electoral urn.
If men are equal before God, they must be equal before the law and have an equal opportunity to earn their living. Brotherhood is a splendid ideal, but only in natural groups such as the family or the native land.
Our Canadian ancestors did not fight in order that their sons loaf about the streets in the cities, living the life of stowaways, not knowing, when they are 20 years old or 30 years old, what to do with their arms and their heads. Did they want us to be servants for foreigners coming here, on a call from us, with the pound sterling or the United States dollar, to enrol Canadians and harness them to their service, exploiting Canadian natural resources to the advantage of London or New York money makers?
The logic of the present system, we find it in mortgages on land won from the forest, in man-made legislation which guarantees that money will draw its salary even if towns and school boards have to be put in trusteeship, private individuals in bankruptcy and farmers out on the road.
When ratepayers pay taxes, they are handing over to the government some well-earned 20220-91^
The Budget-Mr. Latulippe money. Why could they not get in return, the same as the banker, an interest bearing bond?
Where is the logic in all that? With taxes being parallel, loans being possible for the rich, taxes being compulsory for everyone and people being taxed so that interest may be paid to lenders, what happens is that taxes, instead of contributing to a better distribution of wealth, contribute to a higher concentration of wealth.
The purpose of taxation, factor of privation, is to reduce the purchasing power of the public by giving the taxpayer, in exchange for his taxes, a corresponding liability which will have to be paid, since that liability bears interests. If the banker's stroke of the pen deserves interests, the sweat of the worker also deserves interests.
It would be less expensive for the government than the army of employees assigned to the collection of those taxes and the control of that collection. In that way, taxes would operate as interest bearing bonds, and the government would be relieved of a heavy and expensive bureaucracy. But considerations relating to a plan will throw more light on the flagrant injustice of our present financial system by which our governments breathe, act and swear.
Before this dying monster of hypocrisy, covered with debts like purulent and incurable sores, reeking of squalid selfishness, which cannot even be honestly protected by its guardians, what is there to take its place? Collapse into chaos and anarchy while being engulfed in an exasperated destitution?
Mr. Speaker, in conclusion, I am asking the Minister of Finance to tell us, if he can, where we are going, if we are going nowhere, what is wrong and what solution, if any, he has to offer.
I do not hesitate to tell him, supported by most Canadians, that the financial machinery in Canada is out of order and obsolete. The Canadian forests do not refuse to provide Canadians with lumber. The great rivers with their torrential waters are not dried up. It is not the manufacturers, nor the men who refuse to work; it is not the farmers who refuse to produce goods; it is not the land that refuses to yield crops; but all that will go to ruin if everything continues to be dependant on the old heartless financial machinery.
We need a financial machinery beneficial instead of detrimental to the Canadian people, a machinery making money in keeping with progress instead of making debts, a machinery likely to increase the purchasing power instead of decreasing it through heavier taxes which are a burden for everybody. We need a new economy, not an economy of hardship,
1438	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Latulippe but an economy distributing wealth. We must find as many new sources of money as are needed to distribute wealth among everybody.
Canadian finance at the service of Canadians; the wealth of Canada for Canadian families, all families; that is the true meaning of an economy at the service of the human being.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) said in his speech, at the beginning of the session, that the number of unemployed has decreased and that, on the other hand, labour income was much higher in 1963 than in 1962; that the number of jobs had increased tremendously and that the unemployment level in December, taking into account seasonal adjustments, was 5 per cent lower than it had been for many years. He also said that Canadians had made tremendous economic progress in 1963.
I will say to the Prime Minister, in reply, that Canada has never known an increase in social welfare comparable to that of 1963.
In fact, that department's estimates for 1962-63 amounted to $1,099,742,250 whereas in 1963-64 they were only $1,204,910,550, that is an increase of $105,168,300 for the last year. And for 1964-65, the estimates show an even larger increase.
The Prime Minister was careful not to say that the drop in unemployment had not kept pace with the increase in economic activity. In general, the unemployed totalled 7.2 per cent of the active population in 1961, 6 per cent in 1962 and an average of 5 per cent in 1963; and in mid-January this year, there were 466,000 unemployed, that is 7 per cent of the labour force.
However, unemployment is not the same throughout the country. In Quebec, for instance, 9 per cent of the workers are unemployed and, in the maritimes, 12.6 per cent of the labour force are out of work.
It is truly alarming to live under an economic system where at the national level one person out of 15 is unemployed and where one tenth of all Quebec workers and one eighth of the labour population of the maritimes are out of work.
It is our contention that the government has never really tackled the cause of unemployment and of the slow rate of economic growth in Canada. It has just skimmed the problem without ever finding its true causes.
I am convinced that the problem is mainly one of production. We have unemployed workers, idle industries and undeveloped resources. Our first problem is that a large number of Canadians are unable to buy the goods which our economy has produced or could produce.


I will say to the government's face that it is a crime to allow human beings to live under such conditions, when there is an abundance of goods to meet the needs of all classes of society.
Each man, each woman who does not eat enough and, who suffers from cold, each family which is poorly housed, is a living accusation against you, who belong to the old parties, and against the dishonest system that you try to protect with all your might. The day may be not too far off when you will be compelled to take your responsibilities.
The Creditistes are aware of their responsibilities and they fight to provide each individual with his share of progress and knowledge that has been passed on and accumulated from generation to generation, while the old parties have sold our national heritage and the fruit of the labours of generations to strangers. They have even relinquished the control of money and credit in favour of private interests. That is the reason why the people are dispossessed; it is the result of the economic disorder which we experience at the present time.
This is also the exact reason why we do not have a flag yet, since we are economically deprived of the fruits of passed generations. Our government parted with its sovereignty; when one is not master in one's own home, it is rather embarrassing to adopt a flag. That is probably why Liberals have been talking of a flag for 22 years and never adopted one. But we are playing upon people's feelings at each election with St. Jean Baptiste speeches, just like the master speech which the Prime Minister delivered last February 20.
I am quite pleased to say to my hon. friends of the old parties that people are now sufficiently informed not to believe in those speeches any longer but to believe in facts and in results.
The citizens of Canada realize that the old-line parties have seen to it that the people remained unaware of public affairs, of political and economic affairs and of financial affairs. People have been led to believe that democracy is the right to vote accompanied by the right to speak, the right to listen, the right to cheer, even when they are given a raw deal, the sacred right, for the people, to select once every four or five years those whose duty it will be to search through their pockets and put them to sleep.
People are on the verge of having enough of war policies, credit restrictions, austerity programs, excess taxes, money interests which annoy them and take everything away from them, surveys, forms, dictatorship, slavery.
Mr. Speaker, people want us to try and establish in this world a social order in which

man will be able to live decently so that he may reach his full development.
